results.title: Nerode equivalence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. Two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$ when they have the same left quotient, that is, $\{z \in \Sigma^* \mid xz \in L\} = \{z \in \Sigma^* \mid yz \in L\}$.

results.title: The Nerode setoid
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the Nerode setoid of $L$ is the set $\Sigma^*$ of words equipped with Nerode equivalence for $L$, which is reflexive, symmetric and transitive.

results.title: Nerode classes
results.caption: Abbreviation
results.summary: For a language $L$ over an alphabet $\Sigma$, the Nerode classes of $L$ are the elements of the quotient of the set of words over $\Sigma$ by Nerode equivalence for $L$, under which two words $x$ and $y$ are equivalent when they have the same left quotient, that is, when for every word $z$ we have $xz \in L$ if and only if $yz \in L$.

results.title: Continuation characterization of Nerode equivalence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. Two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$ if and only if, for every word $z \in \Sigma^*$, $xz \in L$ holds exactly when $yz \in L$.

results.title: Nerode equivalent words agree on membership
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language. If two words $x$ and $y$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$, then $x \in L$ if and only if $y \in L$.

results.title: Nerode equivalence is a right congruence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$, then for every word $z \in \Sigma^*$ the words $xz$ and $yz$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$.

results.title: Appending a symbol preserves Nerode equivalence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. If two words $x, y \in \Sigma^*$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$, then for every symbol $a \in \Sigma$ the words $xa$ and $ya$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$.

results.title: Appending the empty word preserves the Nerode class
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. For every word $x \in \Sigma^*$, the word $x\varepsilon$ obtained by appending the empty word $\varepsilon$ is Nerode equivalent to $x$ for $L$.

results.title: Nerode class of a word
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a language $L$ and a word $x$, the Nerode class $[x]$ of $x$ is the equivalence class of $x$ under Nerode equivalence for $L$.

results.title: Residual map on Nerode classes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language. The residual map sends the Nerode class $[x]$ of a word $x$ to the left quotient $x^{-1}L = \{ y \mid xy \in L \}$, viewed as an element of the set $\{ w^{-1}L \mid w \text{ a word} \}$ of left quotients of $L$. It is well-defined because Nerode equivalent words have the same left quotient.

results.title: Bijection between Nerode classes and left quotients
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For every language $L$, the map sending the Nerode class $[x]$ of a word $x$ to the left quotient $x^{-1}L = \{ y \mid xy \in L \}$ is a bijection from the set of Nerode classes of $L$ onto the set $\{ w^{-1}L \mid w \text{ a word} \}$ of left quotients of $L$.

results.title: Transition on Nerode classes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$ and $a \in \Sigma$ a symbol. Appending $a$ sends the Nerode class of a word $x$ to the Nerode class of $xa$; this is well defined because Nerode equivalence is preserved by appending a symbol.

results.title: Accepting Nerode classes
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language. The accepting Nerode classes of $L$ are those whose words belong to $L$: the Nerode class $[x]$ of a word $x$ is accepting if and only if $x \in L$. This is well-defined because Nerode equivalent words are either both in $L$ or both outside $L$.

results.title: The Nerode automaton
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. The Nerode automaton of $L$ is the deterministic automaton over $\Sigma$, not necessarily finite, whose states are the Nerode classes of words for $L$, whose start state is the class of the empty word, which on reading a symbol $a \in \Sigma$ moves from the class of a word $x$ to the class of $xa$, and whose accepting states are the classes of the words in $L$.

results.title: The Nerode automaton recognizes its language
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every language $L$, the language accepted by the Nerode automaton of $L$ is exactly $L$.

results.title: Every state of the Nerode automaton is reachable
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every language $L$ and every Nerode class $q$ of $L$, there is a word $x$ such that the Nerode automaton of $L$, started in its start state and reading $x$, ends in the state $q$.

results.title: Finitely many Nerode classes iff finitely many left quotients
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every language $L$, writing $x^{-1}L = \{ y \mid xy \in L \}$ for the left quotient of $L$ by a word $x$, there are finitely many Nerode classes of $L$ if and only if the set $\{ x^{-1}L \mid x \text{ a word} \}$ of left quotients of $L$ is finite.

results.title: Myhill–Nerode theorem, quotient form
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A language $L$ is regular, that is, accepted by some deterministic finite automaton, if and only if $L$ has finitely many Nerode classes.

results.title: Distinguishable words
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language over an alphabet $\Sigma$. Two words $x$ and $y$ over $\Sigma$ are distinguishable by $L$ when there is a word $z$ over $\Sigma$ such that exactly one of $xz$ and $yz$ belongs to $L$.

results.title: Words reaching the same DFA state are Nerode equivalent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA and let $L$ be the language it accepts. If $M$ reaches the same state from its start state on reading the words $x$ and $y$, then $x$ and $y$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$.

results.title: Distinguishable words reach different DFA states
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language and let $M$ be a DFA that accepts exactly $L$. If two words $x$ and $y$ are distinguishable by $L$, then the states that $M$ reaches from its start state on reading $x$ and on reading $y$ are different.

results.title: Equivalent states of a DFA
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Two states $p$ and $q$ of a DFA $M$ are equivalent when they accept the same continuation language: for every word $z$, running $M$ from $p$ on $z$ ends in an accepting state if and only if running $M$ from $q$ on $z$ does.

results.title: Nerode equivalence is equivalence of the reached states
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA and let $L$ be the language it accepts. Two words $x$ and $y$ are Nerode equivalent for $L$ if and only if the states that $M$ reaches from its start state on reading $x$ and on reading $y$ are observationally equivalent, that is, $M$ accepts the same language from both states.

results.title: Residual languages of reachable states
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a DFA $M$ and a state $q$ of $M$, let $L_q$ be the language of words $z$ such that running $M$ from $q$ on $z$ ends in an accepting state. The reachable residuals of $M$ form the set of the languages $L_q$ over all states $q$ that $M$ reaches from its start state on some input word.

results.title: Nerode classes correspond to reachable residuals
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language and let $M$ be a DFA that accepts exactly $L$. This is the bijection from the Nerode classes of $L$ to the reachable residuals of $M$, the languages accepted by $M$ from states it reaches from its start state. It sends the Nerode class of a word $x$ to the left quotient $\{z \mid xz \in L\}$, which is the language $M$ accepts from the state it reaches on reading $x$.

results.title: Representative of a Nerode class
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a language $L$ and a Nerode class $q$ of $L$, the representative of $q$ is a word whose Nerode class is $q$, chosen once and for all.

results.title: Nerode classes to DFA states
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a language $L$ and a DFA $M$ over the same alphabet, this map sends each Nerode class $q$ of $L$ to the state that $M$ reaches from its start state on the chosen representative of $q$.

results.title: Distinct Nerode classes reach distinct states
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $M$ be a DFA that accepts exactly the language $L$. Then the map sending each Nerode class of $L$ to the state that $M$ reaches from its start state on the chosen representative of the class is injective. In particular, $M$ has at least one distinct state for each Nerode class.

results.title: Nerode classes bound the number of DFA states
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language with finitely many Nerode classes, and let $M$ be a DFA with a finite set of states $Q$ that accepts exactly $L$. Then the number of Nerode classes of $L$ is at most $|Q|$.

results.title: Myhill–Nerode lower bound via left quotients
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language and let $M$ be a DFA with a finite set of states $Q$ that accepts exactly $L$. For a word $x$, the left quotient of $L$ by $x$ is the language $\{z \mid xz \in L\}$. Then the number of distinct left quotients of $L$ is at most $|Q|$.

results.title: Equality case of the Nerode state bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language with finitely many Nerode classes, and let $M$ be a DFA with a finite set of states $Q$ that accepts exactly $L$. Send each Nerode class of $L$ to the state that $M$ reaches from its start state on the chosen representative word of the class. Then the number of Nerode classes of $L$ equals $|Q|$ if and only if every state in $Q$ is the image of some Nerode class under this map.

results.title: Strict Nerode state bound
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $L$ be a language with finitely many Nerode classes, and let $M$ be a DFA with a finite set of states $Q$ that accepts exactly $L$. Send each Nerode class of $L$ to the state that $M$ reaches from its start state on the chosen representative word of the class. If some state in $Q$ is not the image of any Nerode class under this map, then the number of Nerode classes of $L$ is strictly less than $|Q|$.

results.title: Reachable state of a DFA
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A state is reachable when some input word reaches it from the start state.

results.title: Accessible DFA
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A DFA is accessible when every state is reachable.

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a list $xs$ over a preorder and a natural number $k$, $k$ is the length of a longest strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$ when some strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$ has length $k$ and every strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$ has length at most $k$. Here a subsequence need not be contiguous, and strictly increasing means that each element is strictly less than every later one.

results.title: Table of the quadratic LIS program
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The table of a list is a list of triples $(y, k, zs)$, built from the right: the empty list has the empty table, and the table of $x$ followed by $rest$ is the table $t$ of $rest$ with the entry $(x, b + 1, w)$ put in front, where $(b, w)$ is the result of the scan of $t$ for entries above $x$. Building the table costs the total cost of these scans.

results.title: Table entry of largest length
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a list $t$ of entries $(y, k, zs)$, where $k$ is a natural number and $zs$ is a list with elements of the same type as $y$, this timed computation returns the pair of $k$ and the list $y$ followed by $zs$ for an entry of $t$ whose $k$ is largest, provided that this $k$ is positive, and returns $0$ and the empty list otherwise (in particular when $t$ is empty). It costs one unit per entry of $t$.

results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a list $x_0, \dots, x_{n-1}$ of elements of a preorder with decidable $<$, this timed computation builds, from the right, a table recording for each position $i$ a length and a strictly increasing subsequence starting with $x_i$ (the longest one, by the recurrence $L_i = 1 + \max \{ L_j : i < j,\ x_i < x_j \}$ with $\max \emptyset = 0$), and returns the stored subsequence of an entry of largest length, or the…

results.title: Cost of the scan for the best entry above a value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a preorder with decidable $<$. For every value $x \in \alpha$ and every list $t$ of entries $(y, k, zs)$, where $y \in \alpha$, $k$ is a natural number and $zs$ is a list over $\alpha$, the scan of $t$ for the best table entry above $x$ costs exactly the length of $t$.

results.title: Running time of the quadratic LIS program
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $xs$ of length $n$ over a preorder, twice the cost of the quadratic longest-increasing-subsequence program on $xs$ equals $n(n + 1)$, so the program costs exactly $n(n + 1)/2$.

results.title: A subsequence starting with $y$ starts at an occurrence of $y$
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For an element $y$ and lists $zs$ and $l$, if the list $y$ followed by $zs$ is a subsequence (not necessarily contiguous) of $l$, then there is a list $s$ such that $y$ followed by $s$ is a suffix of $l$ and $zs$ is a subsequence of $s$.

results.title: Invariant of the LIS table
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A table $t$ of triples $(y, k, zs)$ satisfies the invariant for a list $l$ when every entry $(y, k, zs)$ of $t$ has a list $s$ such that $y$ followed by $s$ is a suffix of $l$ and $(k, zs)$ is a table cell for $y$ followed by $s$, and conversely, for every element $y$ and list $s$ such that $y$ followed by $s$ is a suffix of $l$, some entry $(y, k, zs)$ of $t$ makes $(k, zs)$ a table cell for $y$ followed by $s$.

results.title: The step of the LIS recurrence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $x$ be an element, $rest$ a list, and $t$ a table of triples $(y, k, zs)$ that satisfies the invariant of the LIS table for $rest$. Let $(b, w)$ be the result of the scan of $t$ for entries above $x$. Then $(b + 1, w)$ is a table cell for $x$ followed by $rest$: $w$ is a subsequence of $rest$, the list $x$ followed by $w$ is strictly increasing and has length $b + 1$, and every strictly increasing list $x$…

results.title: Correctness of the quadratic LIS program
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $xs$ over a preorder, the list returned by the quadratic longest-increasing-subsequence program on $xs$ is a subsequence of $xs$, is strictly increasing (each element strictly less than every later one), and is at least as long as every strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$.

results.title: The quadratic LIS program attains the optimal length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $xs$ over a preorder, the length of the list returned by the quadratic longest-increasing-subsequence program on $xs$ is the length of a longest strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$.

results.title: Uniqueness of the longest increasing subsequence length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $xs$ of elements of a preorder and all natural numbers $k$ and $k'$, if both $k$ and $k'$ are the length of a longest strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$, then $k = k'$.

results.title: Correctness of the quadratic LIS program, by length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $xs$ over a preorder and every natural number $k$, the list returned by the quadratic longest-increasing-subsequence program on $xs$ has length $k$ if and only if $k$ is the length of a longest strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$.

results.title: Patience step
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given an array $t$ of tails and an element $x$ over a linear order, let $i$ be the index returned by the lower-bound binary search for $x$ in $t$. If $i$ is less than the size of $t$, the step replaces the entry of $t$ at index $i$ by $x$; otherwise it appends $x$ to $t$. Its cost is the number of comparisons made by the binary search.

results.title: Patience scan
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given an array of tails and a list over a linear order, the patience scan applies the patience step to the elements of the list in order: on the empty list it returns the tails unchanged, and on a list $x$ followed by $xs$ it applies the patience step for $x$ to the tails and then runs the patience scan of $xs$ from the result. Its cost is the total cost of the steps.

results.title: Patience sorting
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a list $xs$ over a linear order, patience sorting runs the patience scan of $xs$ starting from the empty array of tails and returns the size of the resulting array. Its cost is the number of comparisons made by the scan.

results.title: Patience sorting invariant
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: For lists $P$ and $t = (t_0, \dots, t_{m-1})$ over a linear order, the invariant holds for the processed prefix $P$ and the tails $t$ when three conditions hold: $t$ is strictly increasing; for every $k < m$ some strictly increasing subsequence of $P$ of length $k + 1$ has last element $t_k$; and every nonempty strictly increasing subsequence of $P$, of length $\ell$ and with last element $y$, satisfies…

results.title: The patience scan preserves the invariant
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $P$ be a list and $t$ an array of tails over a linear order such that the patience sorting invariant holds for $P$ and the entries of $t$. Then for every list $xs$, the invariant holds for $P$ followed by $xs$ and the entries of the array returned by the patience scan of $xs$ from $t$.

results.title: Correctness of patience sorting
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linear order, the value returned by patience sorting on $xs$ is the length of a longest strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$: some strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$ has this length, and no strictly increasing subsequence of $xs$ is longer.

results.title: Patience sorting agrees with the quadratic dynamic program
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $xs$ over a linear order, the value returned by patience sorting on $xs$ equals the length of the list returned on $xs$ by the quadratic dynamic program for a longest strictly increasing subsequence.

results.title: A patience step grows the tails by at most one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\alpha$ be a linear order. For every array $t$ over $\alpha$ and every element $x \in \alpha$, the array returned by the patience step for $x$ on $t$ has size at most the size of $t$ plus $1$.

results.title: Comparison bound for patience sorting
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $xs$ of length $n$ over a linear order, patience sorting on $xs$ uses at most $n \lceil \log_2 (n + 1) \rceil$ comparisons.

results.title: Splitting off the power of two
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $m > 0$, the two-adic split of $m$ is the pair $(t, u)$ of natural numbers with $m = 2^t u$ and $u$ odd. For $m = 0$ it is $(0, 0)$.

results.title: The Miller–Rabin squaring loop
results.caption: Definition
results.summary:
Fix a modulus $n$. With no squarings remaining, the loop at the current value $x$ reports a witness exactly when $x 
e 1$, at no cost. With $k + 1$ squarings remaining, it costs one modular multiplication and computes $y = x^2  mod n$; it reports a witness if $y = 1$, $x 
e 1$ and $x 
e n - 1$, and otherwise continues at $y$ with $k$ squarings remaining.

results.title: Miller–Rabin witness test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For natural numbers $a$ and $n$, write $n - 1 = 2^t u$ with $u$ odd (here $n - 1$ is truncated at $0$, and $t = u = 0$ when $n \le 1$). The test sets $x_0$ to the result of modular exponentiation of $a$ to the power $u$ modulo $n$, which is $a^u \bmod n$ when $u > 0$ and $1$ when $u = 0$. For $i = 1, \dots, t$ it computes $x_i = x_{i-1}^2 \bmod n$ and returns true as soon as $x_i = 1$, $x_{i-1} \ne 1$ and…

results.title: The Miller–Rabin test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a natural number $n$ and a list of bases $a_1, \dots, a_s$, the test runs the witness test for $n$ on each base in turn. It answers *composite* as soon as some base $a_i$ is a witness to the compositeness of $n$, and *prime* if none is (in particular on the empty list). Its cost is the sum of the costs of the witness tests it runs.

results.title: Cost bound for the Miller–Rabin squaring loop
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all natural numbers $n$, $k$ and $x$, the cost of the squaring loop modulo $n$ started at $x$ with $k$ squarings remaining is at most $k$.

results.title: Cost of the Miller–Rabin witness test
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For natural numbers $a$ and $n$, write $n - 1 = 2^t u$ with $u$ odd (here $n - 1$ is truncated at $0$, and $t = u = 0$ when $n \le 1$). The cost of the witness test on base $a$ and modulus $n$ is at most the cost of the modular exponentiation of $a$ to the power $u$ modulo $n$ plus $t$: at most one multiplication for each of the $t$ squarings.

results.title: The squaring loop modulo a prime finds no witness when it ends at 1
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a prime and let $k$ and $x$ be natural numbers with $x < p$ and $x^{2^k} \bmod p = 1$. Then the squaring loop modulo $p$ started at $x$ with $k$ squarings remaining reports no witness.

results.title: A prime has no Miller–Rabin witnesses in range
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$ be a prime and $a$ a natural number with $0 < a < n$. Then the witness test does not report $a$ as a witness to the compositeness of $n$.

results.title: A Miller–Rabin witness in range proves compositeness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$ and $a$ be natural numbers with $0 < a < n$. If the witness test reports $a$ as a witness to the compositeness of $n$, then $n$ is not prime.

results.title: The Miller–Rabin test never rejects a prime when its bases lie in range
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$ be a prime. For every list of bases $a_1, \dots, a_s$ (possibly empty) with $0 < a_i < n$ for each $i$, the Miller–Rabin test run on $n$ with these bases answers *prime*.

results.title: With bases in range, a composite answer of the Miller–Rabin test is correct
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number and $a_1, \dots, a_s$ a list of bases with $0 < a_i < n$ for each $i$. If the Miller–Rabin test run on $n$ with these bases answers *composite*, then $n$ is not prime.

results.title: The squaring loop reports a witness when it does not end at 1
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$, $k$ and $x$ be natural numbers with $n > 0$, $x < n$ and $x^{2^k} \bmod n \ne 1$. Then the squaring loop modulo $n$ started at $x$ with $k$ squarings remaining reports a witness.

results.title: Fermat witnesses are Miller–Rabin witnesses
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $a$ and $n$ be natural numbers with $n > 1$. If $a^{n-1} \bmod n \ne 1$, that is, $a^{n-1} \not\equiv 1 \pmod{n}$, then the Miller–Rabin witness test on base $a$ and modulus $n$ returns true.

results.title: When the squaring loop finds no witness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$, $k$ and $x$ be natural numbers with $x < n$. If the Miller–Rabin squaring loop modulo $n$, started at $x$ with $k$ squarings to perform, reports no witness, then $x = 1$ or $x^{2^i} \equiv -1 \pmod n$ for some $i < k$.

results.title: What a non-witness satisfies
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n > 1$ and write $n - 1 = 2^t u$ with $u$ odd. If $a$ is a natural number for which the Miller–Rabin witness test $\mathrm{WITNESS}(a, n)$ returns false, then $a^u \equiv 1 \pmod n$, or $a^{2^i u} \equiv -1 \pmod n$ for some $i < t$.

results.title: Non-witnesses pass Fermat's test and are units
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n > 1$ and let $a$ be a natural number such that the witness test $\mathrm{WITNESS}(a, n)$ returns false. Then $a^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ and $a$ is coprime to $n$.

results.title: Non-witnesses of a number
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, the non-witnesses of $n$ form the finite set of bases $a$ with $0 < a < n$ for which the Miller–Rabin witness test $\mathrm{WITNESS}(a, n)$ returns false, that is, the bases that do not witness the compositeness of $n$.

results.title: At most half the bases are non-witnesses when some unit fails Fermat's test
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n > 1$, and suppose some $x$ coprime to $n$ has $x^{n-1} \not\equiv 1 \pmod n$. Then at most $(n - 1)/2$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$.

results.title: At most half the bases are non-witnesses for a Carmichael number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$ be a Carmichael number: $n > 2$, $n$ is not prime, and $b^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ for every $b$ coprime to $n$. Then at most $(n - 1)/2$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$.

results.title: At most half the bases are non-witnesses
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n > 1$ be odd and not prime. Then at most $(n - 1)/2$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$; equivalently, at least $(n - 1)/2$ of them are witnesses to the compositeness of $n$.

results.title: Miller–Rabin answers prime exactly when no base is a witness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$ and every list of bases, the Miller–Rabin test on $n$ with these bases answers *prime* if and only if, for every base $a$ in the list, the witness test $\mathrm{WITNESS}(a, n)$ returns false, that is, $a$ is not a witness to the compositeness of $n$.

results.title: Half error bound for Miller–Rabin with several bases
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n > 1$ be odd and not prime, and let $s$ be a natural number. Among the $(n - 1)^s$ lists $(b_1, \dots, b_s)$ of bases with $0 < b_i < n$, at most $((n - 1)/2)^s$ make the Miller–Rabin test of $n$ with bases $b_1, \dots, b_s$ answer *prime*.

results.title: At most a quarter of the bases are non-witnesses when some unit fails Fermat's test and the modulus is not a prime power
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: At most a quarter of the bases are non-witnesses when some unit fails Fermat's test and the modulus is not a prime power. Let $n > 1$ be odd and not prime, and not of the form $p^e$ with $p$ prime and $e \ge 2$. Suppose some $z$ coprime to $n$ has $z^{n-1} \not\equiv 1 \pmod n$. Then at most $(n - 1)/4$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$.

results.title: At most a quarter of the bases are non-witnesses for a Carmichael number
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$ be a Carmichael number: $n > 2$, $n$ is not prime, and $b^{n-1} \equiv 1 \pmod n$ for every $b$ coprime to $n$. Then at most $(n - 1)/4$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$.

results.title: At most a quarter of the bases are non-witnesses for an odd prime power
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $p$ be a prime and $k \ge 2$ with $p^k$ odd. Then at most $(p^k - 1)/4$ of the bases $1, \dots, p^k - 1$ are non-witnesses for $p^k$.

results.title: At most a quarter of the bases are non-witnesses
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n > 1$ be odd and not prime. Then at most $(n - 1)/4$ of the bases $1, \dots, n - 1$ are non-witnesses for $n$, so one uniformly random base fails to expose $n$ as composite with probability at most $1/4$.

results.title: Quarter error bound for Miller–Rabin with several bases
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n > 1$ be odd and not prime, and let $s$ be a natural number. Among the $(n - 1)^s$ lists $(b_1, \dots, b_s)$ of bases with $0 < b_i < n$, at most $\lfloor (n - 1)/4 \rfloor^s$ make the Miller–Rabin test of $n$ with bases $b_1, \dots, b_s$ answer *prime*.

results.title: Binary constraint satisfaction problem
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A binary constraint satisfaction problem with variables in $X$ and values in $D$ consists of a finite list of directed arcs $(x, y)$ with $x, y \in X$, and, for all variables $x, y$ and values $a, b \in D$, a Boolean saying whether the arc $(x, y)$ allows $x = a$ together with $y = b$.

results.title: Solution of a binary CSP within given domains
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with variables $X$ and values $D$, and give each variable $x$ a finite domain $\mathrm{dom}(x) \subseteq D$. An assignment $\sigma : X \to D$ is a solution of $P$ within $\mathrm{dom}$ when $\sigma(x) \in \mathrm{dom}(x)$ for every variable $x$ and, for every arc $(x, y)$ of $P$, the arc $(x, y)$ allows the pair $(\sigma(x), \sigma(y))$.

results.title: Arc consistency
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Given a binary CSP $P$ and domains $\mathrm{dom}$, an arc $(x, y)$ is consistent when for every value $a \in \mathrm{dom}(x)$ there is a value $b \in \mathrm{dom}(y)$ such that the arc $(x, y)$ allows $x = a$ together with $y = b$.

results.title: Symmetric binary CSP
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A binary constraint satisfaction problem is symmetric when, for all variables $x, y$ and values $a, b$, the constraint on the ordered pair $(x, y)$ allows $x = a$ together with $y = b$ exactly when the constraint on $(y, x)$ allows $y = b$ together with $x = a$.

results.title: Revision of an arc
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with values $D$, $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables, and $x$, $y$ variables. The revision of the arc $(x, y)$ is the set of values $a \in \mathrm{dom}(x)$ that have a support in the domain of $y$: some $b \in \mathrm{dom}(y)$ such that the arc $(x, y)$ allows the pair $(a, b)$.

results.title: In-degree of a variable
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a binary constraint satisfaction problem $P$ and a variable $x$, the in-degree of $x$ is the number of arcs $(z, x)$ of $P$ ending at $x$, counted with multiplicity in the list of arcs of $P$.

results.title: Arcs requeued after a revision
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a binary constraint satisfaction problem $P$ and variables $x$ and $y$, the arcs requeued after revising $(x, y)$ are the arcs $(z, x)$ of $P$ with $z \neq y$, in their order in the list of arcs of $P$.

results.title: A shrinking revision lowers the potential

results.title: AC-3 on the whole problem
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a binary CSP $P$ with finitely many variables and domains $\mathrm{dom}$, AC-3 on the whole problem is AC-3 run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with the queue initialized to the arc list of $P$; it returns the final domains together with the number of revisions performed.

results.title: AC-3 only shrinks domains
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a binary CSP $P$ with finitely many variables, domains $\mathrm{dom}$, a queue $q$ of pairs of variables and a variable $v$, the domain of $v$ returned by AC-3 run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with queue $q$ is a subset of $\mathrm{dom}(v)$.

results.title: Revision keeps solution values
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem, $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables and $\sigma$ a solution of $P$ within $\mathrm{dom}$. For every arc $(x, y)$ of $P$, the value $\sigma(x)$ lies in the revision of the arc $(x, y)$ with respect to $\mathrm{dom}$.

results.title: No solution is lost
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with finitely many variables, $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables, and $q$ a queue of arcs each of which is an arc of $P$. Then every solution $\sigma$ of $P$ within $\mathrm{dom}$ is also a solution of $P$ within the domains returned by AC-3 started from $\mathrm{dom}$ with queue $q$.

results.title: Solutions survive AC-3
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with finitely many variables and $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables. If $\sigma$ is a solution of $P$ within $\mathrm{dom}$, then for every variable $v$ the value $\sigma(v)$ lies in the domain of $v$ returned by AC-3 run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with all arcs of $P$ queued.

results.title: An emptied domain rules out solutions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $P$ be a binary constraint satisfaction problem with finitely many variables and $\mathrm{dom}$ finite domains for its variables. If AC-3, run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with all arcs of $P$ queued, returns the empty domain for some variable $v$, then no assignment $\sigma$ is a solution of $P$ within $\mathrm{dom}$.

results.title: AC-3 makes every arc consistent
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: AC-3 makes every arc consistent, for constraints given symmetrically on both orientations of an arc and arcs between distinct variables.

results.title: AC-3 revisions are bounded by the potential
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a binary CSP $P$ with finitely many variables, domains $\mathrm{dom}$ and a queue $q$ of pairs of variables, the number of revisions AC-3 performs from $\mathrm{dom}$ with queue $q$ is at most the potential $\ell + \sum_x |\mathrm{dom}(x)| \cdot \mathrm{indeg}(x)$, where $\ell$ is the length of $q$ and $\mathrm{indeg}(x)$ is the number of entries of the arc list of $P$ ending at $x$.

results.title: Bound on the number of AC-3 revisions
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a binary CSP $P$ with finitely many variables and initial domains $\mathrm{dom}$, AC-3 run from $\mathrm{dom}$ with every arc of $P$ queued performs at most $m + \sum_x |\mathrm{dom}(x)| \cdot \mathrm{indeg}(x)$ revisions, where $m$ is the length of the arc list of $P$ and $\mathrm{indeg}(x)$ is the number of entries of that list ending at $x$.

results.title: Profile hidden Markov model
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: A profile HMM with `L` consensus columns over the alphabet `α`, with weights in `R`. `trans k s t` is the weight of a transition from the state of type `s` at node `k` (`0 ≤ k ≤ L`; node `0` is the begin state, read as type `M`) to a state of type `t`: to `M` or `D` at node `k + 1`, or to `I` at node `k`. `stop s` is the weight of the transition from the state of type `s` at node `L` to the end state.

results.title: HMMER Plan 7 restrictions
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: HMMER's Plan 7 restrictions (Eddy 1998): no delete-to-insert and no insert-to-delete transitions, and no insert states at node `0` (the begin state) or node `L`.

results.title: Weight of a path through a profile HMM
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The weight of a path through the model, given as an alignment `A` of the sequence to the columns: the product of its transition and emission weights from the begin state to the end state.

results.title: Forward value of a sequence under a profile HMM
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The forward value of a sequence `x`: the total weight of all paths through the model that emit `x` (`forward_eq_sum`), by the recursion on one residue and one column.

results.title: Forward computes the total path weight
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The sum, over all alignments of `x` to the columns `[1, …, L]` (all paths through the model emitting `x`, each once), of the path weights.

results.title: Viterbi value of a sequence under a profile HMM
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The Viterbi value of a sequence `x`: the value selected by the max recursion (`pathProb_le_viterbi`, `exists_pathProb_eq_viterbi`). Under nonnegative weights it is the largest weight of a path through the model emitting `x`.

results.title: Nonnegative weights of a profile HMM
results.caption: Structure
results.summary: Nonnegative transition and emission weights (the transitions to the end state may have any sign: the Viterbi bound does not need them).

results.title: Nonnegative profile HMM gives a nonnegative alignment automaton
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A profile HMM with nonnegative weights is a nonnegative alignment automaton.

results.title: Every path weighs at most the Viterbi value
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Every path weighs at most the Viterbi value.

results.title: The Viterbi value is attained
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Some path (alignment of `x` to the profile) has weight equal to the Viterbi value. Under nonnegative weights this attained value is the largest path weight (`pathProb_le_viterbi`); without that hypothesis attainment alone does not imply maximality.

results.title: Pseudocount emission estimate of a match state
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The emission estimate of a match state from the residues `col` that a multiple alignment places in its column (gaps omitted), with pseudocounts `pc` (Durbin et al., chapter 5; Laplace's rule is `pc = 1`): `(count a + pc a) / (|col| + ∑ b, pc b)`.

results.title: Pseudocount emission estimates sum to one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With positive pseudocounts, the estimated emissions sum to one.

results.title: Pseudocount emission estimates are positive
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With positive pseudocounts, every residue gets a positive emission estimate, including residues absent from the column.
